extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters / patent attorneys / patent agents preparing patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patent claims, description, drawings and abstract so the application is clear, internally consistent, enables practice by a person skilled in the art, and is adapted to differing national practices. Includes recommended order of drafting, section-by-section standards, and wording tips to avoid narrowing or losing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — starting point and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts generally interpret claim terms by giving them their ordinary meaning to a person skilled in the art; only thereafter will courts consult the description and prosecution history to see whether terms were given different or special meanings. Particularly in the United States, courts increasingly use dictionaries when construing claims and interpret ordinary terms accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims and description do not clearly communicate a specific meaning, courts will refer to the general meaning to a skilled person. Technical dictionaries, encyclopedias, treatises and expert testimony may be used to establish field-specific meanings. Draft with awareness that courts begin from ordinary meaning and then look to intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define new or ambiguous claim terms in the description
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent application creates a new term, when several different meanings for a term are possible and only one is meant or when the meaning of a term may be ambiguous, it should sensibly be defined in the description section of the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description can act as a glossary of special claim terminology. Aim for a self-contained application that can be understood without external context to avoid reliance on dictionaries or treatises in later construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft claims as if no doctrine of equivalents exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be drafted literally, giving terms their ordinary and customary meaning to a person skilled in the relevant art, rather than relying on the doctrine of equivalents to provide protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional tip: to deter imitators or litigate effectively, draft claims as though equivalents do not exist. Avoid relying on uncertain equivalents regimes across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — jurisdictional variability and prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents provides legal protection beyond literal claim words in some jurisdictions, but its scope and standards vary significantly from country to country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent drafters must learn the regime applicable in jurisdictions of interest, including whether communications during prosecution can foreclose application of the doctrine (prosecution history estoppel). Be careful in responses to office actions that might limit later arguments on equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare claims before other parts of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting first the broadest main claim(s) reciting the inventive features is an efficient way of formulating the essential inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drafting the background art first (risk: too long/detailed). Drafting claims first helps identify what embodiments, examples and drawings are needed to support the claimed invention and prevents extraneous limiting elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended order of drafting and iterative review
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested workflow: (i) draft broadest main claim(s); (ii) draft title, technical field, background and summary; (iii) draft brief description of figures, detailed description of embodiments and drawings; (iv) revisit and refine claims; (v) check drawings and description for support, consistency and appropriate disclosure of claim terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application is rarely drafted strictly sequentially; drafting is iterative. Revisit claims after drafting description/drawings to spot unnecessary or inadequately supported claim elements and to narrow or add claims as needed to address prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT / description section headings and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: International (PCT) applications are typically headed: 'Title of invention', 'Technical field', 'Background art', 'Summary of invention' or 'Disclosure of invention', 'Best mode for carrying out the invention' / 'Brief description of drawings', 'Description of embodiments', 'Industrial applicability' (if relevant), 'Sequence listing' (if relevant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow jurisdictional formats; use the headings appropriate to where protection is sought. PCT expects this structure unless another approach presents the substance more economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title of invention — breadth and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: The title should describe the subject matter of the invention broadly, yet concisely. Avoid being overly narrow so as not to unduly limit implied scope, but make the subject matter sufficiently indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many drafters adopt a broad title because the title may be published soon. Note jurisdictional preferences: e.g., in the United States 'title' is preferred to 'title of invention' to avoid narrowing claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical field — short, general, non-inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical field should recite the field to which the invention pertains in a short paragraph (two or three sentences) stating the general technical field in which the reader is expected to have expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not identify the inventive concept or features in this section; it should indicate general classification only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background art — briefly set context and state the problem, avoid solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Background art should set out briefly the state of the art in the field and identify the problem the invention solves; include only the closest prior art accessible to the public before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lengthy historical accounts and modifiers like 'well-known' or 'common'. Be cautious about admitting prior art (applicant-admitted prior art). Do not describe the solution (invention) in the background; if the problem itself is new, reflect its absence in prior art rather than describing the solution. Avoid 'objects of the invention' statements when possible because they can limit interpretation or fuel fraud arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation of prior art references — check jurisdictional requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions do not require listing specific prior art in the background; others (e.g., Japan) require applicants to describe and list at least one prior art reference known prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the common application format (CAF) guidance: a list of prior art documents may be positioned in the description rather than background. Double-check jurisdictional rules before drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of invention — outline full scope and advantages but avoid absolutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary should outline what has been invented, in its full scope, and explain how the inventor has overcome the background problem; often prepared by turning independent claims into paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include advantageous effects to support inventive step but avoid absolute expressions ('fully eliminated')—use relative expressions ('reduced', 'lower'). Do not produce a broad meta-summary that goes beyond the claims (risk: suggests additional prior art or incomplete disclosure). Check jurisdictional preferences for headings (e.g., use 'summary' rather than 'summary of invention' in the US).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief description of drawings — state what each figure represents and avoid limiting language
rubrics_metrics.description: State what each drawing figure represents and how drawings relate to one another; define drawing types and visual perspectives and briefly note what each figure depicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since drawings often illustrate embodiments rather than general principles, consider starting the brief description with a statement that drawings are illustrative of embodiments only and not of 'the invention' to avoid limiting claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of embodiments — provide enabling, reproducible disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: This section explains various embodiments/examples of the claimed invention; it expands the earlier sections and provides sufficient explanation that a person skilled in the art could reproduce, use and understand the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie the description closely to drawings (use reference numerals). Ensure the disclosure is complete at filing because substantive amendment to add new technical matter is not permitted later. Provide sufficient detail so claims can be narrowed during prosecution to avoid prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure sufficiency of disclosure at filing — cannot add new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of embodiments cannot be substantively amended after the filing date to include new technical disclosure; the application must be sufficient and complete on filing day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the description to reflect inventor-provided material, enable reproduction by skilled persons, and provide depth to allow later claim narrowing if necessary. If insufficient, client may need a new application, risking loss of original filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and consistency — tie abstract terms to embodiments and provide alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: If claims use an abstract term, the description should use the same term but tie it to specific embodiments and provide alternative examples (e.g., list a horn, siren, buzzer as possible 'warning devices').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency across the application reduces ambiguity. Use plain technical language rather than jargon to aid understanding and translation. Providing alternative examples supports broader claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed subject matter — balance inclusion vs dedicating to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters must balance the risk of too bare a description against disclosing too much unclaimed subject matter, which may be considered dedicated to the public if not claimed later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally err on the side of inclusion because missing detail at filing cannot be added later. Be mindful of unity of invention rules; unclaimed inventions lacking unity may require divisional applications rather than post-filing amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the word 'invention' in the description — avoid unnecessary narrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrases like 'the invention is …'; instead use 'an embodiment of the invention' or 'an exemplification of the invention' to preserve broad interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating 'the invention is X' may unnecessarily narrow claimed scope; framing as an embodiment helps ensure the description is read as illustrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known features — omission of well-known material is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters need not include well-known material necessary to make or use the product associated with the claimed invention unless the invention modifies that known feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent application does not have to be a full blueprint; omitting routine, well-known steps or features is acceptable and sometimes preferable to avoid cluttering the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding discussions that limit claims — condition contextual descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When including drawings or context, condition discussions so they do not become limiting (i.e., part of the claim) and avoid language that would narrow claims unintentionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with language choices throughout the application because wording can have consequences in prosecution and litigation. Avoid descriptions that imply essentiality unless intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absolute words unless truly essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Words such as 'must' or 'always' should be used only when they precisely and accurately indicate essential features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute words can create unintended essential limitations. Professional tip: compile a list of absolute words to find and replace before finalizing the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred/optional features — describe as such and recite advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Features in dependent claims should be described as preferred or optional embodiments; otherwise they may be regarded as essential features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recite advantages of preferred features to support later amendments or opposition proceedings. Note: in the United States, practitioners often avoid discussing 'preferred' embodiments because case law disfavors finding infringement where accused products lack preferred features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience awareness — draft for multiple potential readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications have multiple audiences: patent examiners, judges, the client/inventor, competitors, potential infringers and investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the inventor understands the application. Remember investors may scrutinize portfolios; draft so the document communicates clearly to technical and legal stakeholders.
